strengths: Novel theoretical framework analyzing FIM through low-dimensional 'core spaces' of probability distributions, with elegant spectral analysis of the statistical simplex (Theorem 1)
Rigorous mathematical treatment with sound proofs using appropriate techniques (Cauchy interlacing, Löwner partial order, spectral analysis)
Strong theoretical guarantees for Hutchinson-based estimator: proven unbiased with coefficient of variation bounded by √2, contrasted with unbounded variance of MC estimators
Computational efficiency: requires only one backward pass, matching classification loss gradient computation cost
Comprehensive theoretical coverage: multiple bound variants (full, diagonal, block-diagonal, low-rank) systematically developed
Clear presentation with well-structured exposition and detailed proofs in appendices
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: only density visualizations on DistilBERT without quantitative analysis; no downstream task evaluation showing improvement in optimization convergence, training dynamics, or generalization
No comparative benchmarks against existing methods (KFAC, low-rank approximations, block-diagonal methods); missing computational cost and scalability analysis

Unclear practical utility: deterministic bounds are loose in practice (Figure 1); paper does not justify when to use bounds vs. the proposed Hutchinson estimator, nor clarify practical differences in applications

Bounds have limited practical value: upper bounds error scales with σ_C² (unbounded in general); lower bounds error vanishes only as p approaches one-hot vector (not typical during training), and requires expensive power iteration

Limited methodological novelty: Hutchinson's trace estimator is well-established; application to FIM is relatively straightforward given prior MC analysis; main novelty is spectral analysis of simplex with somewhat limited scope
No algorithm or practical method proposed: paper explicitly states 'methodologies on real applications...are not developed here and left as meaningful future work,' significantly limiting impact

Scope restrictions: analysis limited to classification with softmax outputs; extensions to other parametric families only mentioned; no training dynamics analysis or investigation of when bounds are tight/loose
Power iteration overhead for computing λ_C, v_C adds O(MC|D_x|) complexity, potentially negating claimed efficiency gains
Reproducibility concerns: no code provided, some experimental details vague (e.g., why 128 samples?), hardware specifications relegated to appendix

strengths: Elegant theoretical framework unifying analysis of low-dimensional core space (probability simplex) with high-dimensional neuromanifold via pullback tensors
Rigorous mathematical development with comprehensive theoretical results (Theorems 1-2, Lemmas 2-5, Propositions 6-14) and detailed proofs
Practical Hutchinson-based estimator with guaranteed variance bounds (Std ≤ √2·Fᵢᵢ), computationally efficient requiring only single backward pass
Systematic comparison of multiple FIM approximation schemes with explicit error characterizations and clear guidance on applicability
Convincing motivation for Hutchinson over Monte Carlo by demonstrating unbounded coefficient of variation in naive MC (Section 4.1)
Well-organized presentation with logical progression and careful attention to technical detail (e.g., clever use of detach() in Eq. 2)
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: only density visualizations on DistilBERT for two tasks, no optimization experiments, no downstream applications demonstrating practical utility, no empirical variance studies comparing theory to practice
Deterministic bounds are loose in practice (Figure 1 shows upper bound 22.410 vs true value 12.165 in some cases) and computationally limited (upper bound requires computing all C classes)

Incomplete coefficient of variation analysis: while diagonal entries are bounded, off-diagonal entries have arbitrarily large CV (Lemma 5), and practical significance of √2 bound unclear without empirical studies
Limited algorithmic novelty: Hutchinson's trick is well-established; main contribution is careful variance analysis. Power iteration adds O(M|Dx|C) computational cost not fully justified

Narrow applicability restricted to classification with softmax/sigmoid; singularity of pullback metric mentioned only in footnote without proper treatment; no discussion of modern large-scale architectures
Missing comparisons with related methods: no empirical comparison with Kronecker-factored approximations [16,18] or recent FIM approximation work despite citation
Lack of ablation studies on algorithmic choices (power iteration steps, number of Hutchinson samples, dataset sizes), and no evidence these estimators improve optimization over baselines
Authors acknowledge in conclusion that 'new deep learning optimizer, are not developed here and left as meaningful future work'—critical limitation for demonstrating practical impact

strengths: Solid theoretical analysis of FIM spectrum via core space geometry, with novel envelope-based bounds depending on output probability order statistics
Practical Hutchinson-based estimator achieving unbiased estimates with bounded variance (CV ≤ √2) computable in single backward pass, addressing limitations of Monte Carlo methods
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple modalities (NLP, vision, audio) and large pretrained models, with appropriate metrics for small FIM magnitudes
Clear presentation with careful derivations and complete proofs; extends information-geometric understanding of neural network parameter spaces
weaknesses: Critical gap: Paper explicitly acknowledges lack of downstream applications, stating 'results address novel computation of F but are not directly piped into a downstream application.' No experiments demonstrate that better FIM estimates improve optimization, pruning, or generalization

Limited novelty: Pullback metric connection is prior work (Sun 2020); Hutchinson's trace estimator is from 1990; similar application to Hessian appears in AdaHessian. Main contribution is applying known techniques to FIM without strong evidence of necessity

Weak bound tightness: Upper bound error is guaranteed ≥ 1/C (Lemma 3); Proposition 7 shows error remains non-zero when p approaches one-hot; Proposition 8 error vanishes only for one-hot distributions, limiting practical relevance

Incomplete experimental validation: Limited baselines (only empirical FIM and MC FIM); missing comparisons with practical methods like KFAC; only ~20% RelMAE for Hutchinson's estimate without validation that this accuracy level suffices for applications; small FIM computation scale (128 batches)

Practical guidance lacks clarity: F^LR methods ~2× slower with convergence depending on spectral gap γ; fixed T=30 power iterations unjustified; F^LR/F^LR(2) work only on fine-tuned models (Table 2), limiting applicability to pretrained+random head scenarios
